title: Peri-Implantitis: Causes, Prevention, and Treatment Principles
metaDescription: A clinical guide to peri-implantitis: what causes it, how to spot early signs, prevention strategies, and current treatment principles for implants.
excerpt: Peri-implantitis is an inflammatory condition that threatens the bone around dental implants. Learn its causes, early warning signs, prevention, and treatment principles.
heroImageAlt: Illustration of a dental implant showing inflamed peri-implant tissue and bone loss around the implant neck
bodyHtml:
Introduction

Dental implants have become a predictable, long-serving option for replacing missing teeth, but they are not immune to biological complications. One of the most clinically significant of these is peri-implantitis, an inflammatory condition that affects the soft and hard tissues surrounding an osseointegrated implant and, if left unmanaged, can lead to progressive bone loss and eventual implant failure. For both dental professionals and informed patients, understanding how this condition develops, how it can be prevented, and how it is currently managed is essential to protecting the long-term investment that implant therapy represents. This article reviews the causes, prevention strategies, and treatment principles of peri-implant disease from an evidence-informed, clinical perspective relevant to practice in Ontario and across Canada.

Understanding Peri-Implant Disease

Peri-implant disease exists along a spectrum, and distinguishing between its stages is central to appropriate management. The condition is broadly divided into two entities that differ mainly in whether supporting bone has been affected.

Peri-Implant Mucositis

Peri-implant mucositis is a reversible inflammatory process confined to the soft tissue (mucosa) around an implant, without loss of supporting bone. Clinically, it typically presents as redness, swelling, and bleeding on gentle probing. Because the inflammation has not yet progressed to the bone, mucositis is generally considered a treatable precursor stage. Recognizing and addressing it early is one of the most effective ways to prevent progression to the more serious condition.

Peri-Implantitis Defined

Peri-implantitis describes inflammation of the peri-implant tissues accompanied by progressive loss of the supporting bone. It is generally characterized by bleeding or suppuration on probing, increased probing depths compared with earlier baseline measurements, and radiographic evidence of bone loss beyond the changes expected during initial healing and remodelling. Unlike mucositis, the structural changes seen in peri-implantitis are not fully reversible, which is why prevention and early detection carry so much weight. Patients who understand the difference are often better partners in their own long-term care of their dental implants.

Causes and Risk Factors

Peri-implantitis is widely understood to be driven primarily by bacterial biofilm (plaque) accumulating at the implant-tissue interface, producing a host inflammatory response. However, the clinical picture is rarely explained by biofilm alone. A combination of patient-related, implant-related, and maintenance-related factors influences who develops disease and how quickly it progresses.

Biofilm and Plaque Accumulation

As with natural teeth and gum disease, the bacterial biofilm that gathers around an implant is the central initiating factor. When plaque is not disrupted regularly, the resulting inflammatory response can extend toward the bone. Many of the same principles that apply to recognizing gum disease warning signs apply to the tissues around implants, which is why consistent plaque control is foundational.

History of Periodontitis

Individuals with a history of periodontal disease are generally considered to be at higher risk for peri-implant complications. The susceptibility that contributed to tooth loss in the first place does not disappear once implants are placed, so patients with treated periodontitis warrant closer monitoring and a structured maintenance program.

Smoking and Systemic Factors

Smoking is frequently cited as a modifiable risk factor that can impair tissue response and healing. Poorly controlled diabetes and other systemic conditions that affect inflammatory regulation and wound healing may also contribute. These factors do not necessarily preclude implant therapy, but they influence case selection, informed consent, and the intensity of follow-up care.

Implant and Restorative Factors

Technical and restorative elements play a meaningful role. Residual cement left subgingivally after cementing a crown, restorations that make home cleaning difficult, implant malpositioning, and prostheses that do not allow access for hygiene can all create an environment where biofilm persists. Occlusal overload is sometimes discussed as a contributing factor, though its precise role continues to be studied. Thoughtful implant treatment planning that anticipates maintenance needs is an important preventive step long before a complication can arise.

Recognizing the Warning Signs

Peri-implant disease can be deceptively quiet in its early stages, and implants do not transmit sensation the way natural teeth do, so patients may not feel the dull signals that sometimes accompany tooth problems. This makes professional monitoring and patient awareness especially important.

Clinical Indicators

Common signs that merit evaluation include bleeding when brushing or probing around the implant, redness or swelling of the surrounding gum tissue, the presence of pus (suppuration), a gradual increase in probing depth, gum recession exposing implant threads, or in advanced cases, implant mobility. Unlike some natural-tooth conditions, discomfort is not always present, and the absence of pain should not be interpreted as the absence of a problem.

The Role of Radiographs

Because bone changes cannot be seen directly, radiographs taken at appropriate intervals are a key diagnostic tool. Comparing current images against a baseline taken after the restoration was delivered allows the clinician to distinguish normal early remodelling from pathological, progressive bone loss. For patients who have questions about imaging, understanding how the safety of routine dental x-rays is managed can help put periodic monitoring in context.

Comparing Peri-Implant Mucositis and Peri-Implantitis

The table below summarizes the clinical distinctions that guide diagnosis and management decisions. These are general patterns rather than rigid thresholds, and diagnosis should always rest on a full clinical and radiographic assessment.

FeaturePeri-Implant MucositisPeri-Implantitis
Tissue involvedSoft tissue (mucosa) onlySoft tissue and supporting bone
Bone lossAbsentPresent and progressive
Bleeding on probingTypically presentTypically present, often with suppuration
ReversibilityGenerally reversible with treatmentBone changes not reversible; aim is to arrest progression
Primary management focusBiofilm removal and improved hygieneDecontamination, possible surgery, ongoing maintenance

Prevention Principles

Because the structural damage of peri-implantitis cannot be fully undone, prevention is the most valuable strategy available. Prevention is a shared responsibility between the patient, the restorative team, and the surgical provider, and it begins well before any sign of disease appears.

Daily Home Care

Effective, consistent plaque control around implants is the cornerstone of prevention. This includes thorough brushing and appropriate interdental cleaning tailored to the implant restoration. Patients often benefit from guidance on proper flossing technique and on specialized aids such as interdental brushes or water flossers where access is limited. The goal is to disrupt biofilm reliably without traumatizing the surrounding tissue.

Professional Maintenance

Scheduled professional maintenance appointments allow the team to assess tissue health, measure probing depths, review radiographs over time, and remove deposits with implant-appropriate instruments. For patients with implants, these visits function much like structured periodontal maintenance and are not optional extras but an integral part of long-term implant care. The recall interval should be individualized based on risk, with higher-risk patients seen more frequently. In many Ontario practices, patients seeking coordinated periodontal and implant care at Smile Dental Arts Centre in Markham are placed on a tailored maintenance schedule that reflects their individual risk profile.

Risk Factor Management

Addressing modifiable risks meaningfully reduces the likelihood of disease. Supporting patients in smoking cessation, encouraging good control of systemic conditions such as diabetes, and ensuring that restorations are designed for cleanability all contribute. Where cement-retained crowns are used, careful removal of any excess cement is an important technical safeguard against future inflammation.

Treatment Principles

When peri-implant disease is identified, treatment is generally approached in a staged manner, beginning with less invasive measures and escalating as needed based on the response. The overarching aim is to control infection, halt further bone loss, and establish conditions that the patient and team can maintain over time. It is important to note that outcomes vary between individuals, and no approach can promise complete resolution in every case.

Non-Surgical Management

Initial management typically focuses on mechanical disruption and removal of biofilm and deposits from the implant surface using instruments and techniques designed to avoid damaging the implant. Reinforcement of home care, correction of contributing factors, and adjunctive measures such as antiseptic agents may be employed. Non-surgical therapy is often sufficient for peri-implant mucositis and is an essential first phase for peri-implantitis, even when surgery is ultimately required.

Surgical Management

When non-surgical measures do not adequately control established peri-implantitis, surgical intervention may be considered to gain access to the affected implant surface for thorough decontamination. Depending on the defect, the surgical approach may aim to reduce pockets and reshape tissue, or to regenerate lost bone using grafting materials and membranes where the defect morphology is favourable. The choice of technique depends on the extent and shape of the bone loss, the implant position, and overall patient factors. The principles involved share common ground with other procedures discussed in bone grafting around dental implants.

When an Implant Cannot Be Saved

In advanced cases where bone loss is severe, the implant is mobile, or infection cannot be controlled, removal of the implant may become the most appropriate course. This is not a failure of effort so much as a recognition of biological limits, and it allows the site to heal before considering future options. Discussing these possibilities during consent, before treatment begins, helps patients form realistic expectations.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is peri-implantitis the same as gum disease around natural teeth?

The two conditions share important similarities, including a biofilm-driven inflammatory process and the risk of bone loss, but they are not identical. The tissues around implants differ structurally from those around natural teeth, which affects how disease progresses and how it is managed. Many of the warning signs, however, overlap, which is why an understanding of periodontal health is relevant to implant patients.

Can peri-implantitis be reversed?

The earlier, soft-tissue-only stage known as peri-implant mucositis can often be reversed with prompt treatment and improved hygiene. Once bone loss has occurred in established peri-implantitis, that structural loss cannot be fully restored. The realistic goal of treatment is to stop further progression and stabilize the implant, with results that vary from person to person.

How is peri-implantitis diagnosed?

Diagnosis relies on a combination of clinical assessment and imaging. A clinician evaluates probing depths, bleeding or suppuration on probing, and tissue appearance, then compares current radiographs against an earlier baseline to identify progressive bone loss. No single sign confirms the diagnosis on its own; it is the overall picture that matters.

How can I lower my risk?

Consistent daily plaque control, attending individualized maintenance appointments, not smoking, managing systemic health conditions, and ensuring your restoration is designed for easy cleaning all help reduce risk. Reporting any bleeding, swelling, or changes around an implant promptly allows earlier intervention, when management tends to be more straightforward.

Conclusion

Peri-implantitis represents one of the principal biological challenges to the long-term success of dental implants, but it is a condition in which knowledge translates directly into protection. Because the bone loss it causes cannot be fully reversed, the emphasis falls heavily on prevention through meticulous home care, individualized professional maintenance, and management of modifiable risk factors. When disease does develop, a staged approach that begins with decontamination and may extend to surgical therapy offers a path to arresting progression, though outcomes differ between patients and cannot be guaranteed. For patients in Ontario considering or living with implants, partnering with an attentive dental team and keeping regular maintenance appointments remains the most reliable way to safeguard implant health over the years ahead.
